name: Amira Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at a copper mine, what we call an LHD, which stands for load-haul-dump. It's a low, long machine with a bucket on the front that scoops broken rock from where they've blasted and carries it to the ore pass, a shaft that drops it down to the crusher. Day shift I'm in the cage going down at half six, then it's about nine hours of mucking out drawpoints eight hundred metres underground. What I love is when you get a good rhythm going, bucket full every time, no hang-ups. What wears me out is the noise and the dust and the fact that you can't see the sky for the whole shift in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what about life outside the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Tomás, my partner, he teaches year four at the primary school on Hill Road. We rent a nice place and we've got a fair bit saved, about ten months, plus some shares my dad helped me start when I was nineteen. I'm also the health and safety rep for my crew, which means I'm the one who goes to the company when something's not right underground. I use ChatGPT now and then to tidy up my safety reports, because writing isn't my strong point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to fixing the stuff that actually matters, like the ventilation on level twelve. At the crib room, which is our lunch room underground, people would have a laugh about all the money the company spent on AI consultants. I wouldn't post much online, I mostly just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it wouldn't change much for me. The AI hype was never really about my loader, it was about office stuff. The tele-remote loaders, where someone drives them from a room on the surface, those would keep coming slowly whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd keep using the chat tool for my safety reports because it saves me an hour a week, and I'd keep putting a bit into my shares each month. As safety rep I'd keep pushing for the remote loaders on the dangerous drawpoints, because nobody should be standing under bad ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit relieved for my mates in the office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for remote loaders yourself. That's unusual for someone in your seat.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago a guy on C crew, Marco, got a rock through his cab on a drawpoint that had been checked. He was okay, broken collarbone, but I was the one who wrote that report. If a machine can go under bad ground instead of Marco, I'm not going to stand in front of it just to save my own seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to be the person driving it from the surface?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, once I'd seen a few others do it and liked it. My friend Jess went up to the remote room at the other shaft and she says your back hurts less but you miss the crew. I'd want to try it before I decided.

S0.say: She'd say good, let's get back to real problems like the ventilation on level twelve. She'd laugh with the crew about the company's AI consultants but wouldn't post much online.
S0.think: She thinks the AI hype was always about office jobs, not her loader. Tele-remote loaders would keep arriving slowly whatever happens with the chat tools.
S0.do: Keeps working as now, keeps using a chat tool for her safety reports and keeps adding to her shares each month. As safety rep, keeps pushing for remote loaders on the most dangerous drawpoints.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved for friends in office jobs.
S0.quote: If a machine can go under bad ground instead of Marco, I'm not going to stand in front of it just to save my own seat.
S0.fieldNote: Amira's safety rep role shapes everything: she actively wants machines on dangerous ground because of Marco's accident, even at a cost to her own seat. She's open to the remote room but wants to hear from people like Jess first. She already uses AI lightly, for writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that if the company's going to automate, it has to come with training and no forced redundancies, and I'd say it at the safety committee too. With friends I'd say this is what unions are for. Online I might share a petition, that's about my limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my loader job becomes a remote job within five years, and the crew shrinks from eight to three. I'm average at what I do, not the best, so I wouldn't assume I'm one of the three. But I'd have savings and there are other mines nearby, so I'd land somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once two or three people from my crew had done the tele-remote course and said it was fine, I'd sign up for it, probably in the second year. I'd lift my savings a bit, from ten months to a year. As safety rep I'd push for a rule that remote machines and people never work the same level at the same time, because mixed traffic is where people get hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, more like I need to keep my eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to worry and then lie awake doing sums anyway. He'd say his kids at school will be fine because nobody wants a robot teaching nine-year-olds. I'd tell him the copper still has to come out of the ground. It just might not need me to bring it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try the course first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first lot always get the buggy version. I watched the first tele-remote trial, the camera kept fogging up and the guy got blamed for the delays. Let the keen ones find the problems, then I'll go.

S1.say: She'd say any automation has to come with training and no forced redundancies, at work and at the safety committee. With friends she'd say this is what unions are for, and she might share a petition online.
S1.think: She thinks her loader job becomes a remote job within five years, with the crew cut from eight to three. She's average, so she wouldn't assume she's kept, but savings and nearby mines mean she'd land somewhere.
S1.do: Signs up for the tele-remote course in the second year, once two or three crewmates say it works. Lifts savings to about a year and pushes for a rule keeping remote machines and people off the same level at the same time.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful rather than scared.
S1.quote: I'd tell him the copper still has to come out of the ground. It just might not need me to bring it out.
S1.fieldNote: She's openly the 'second wave' person: she watched a buggy first trial and doesn't want to be blamed for teething problems. Her worries about safety in mixed traffic are practical and specific. She'd reassure Tomás and then lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying the government has to step in, fast, with income support for everyone who's pushed out, because two years is no time. At the safety committee I'd be asking who checks the robots' work, because AI that's 'as good as a person' still needs someone accountable. Online I'd be sharing a lot more than petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone in two years and so are most of the jobs I'd move to. The nearby mines would all be doing the same thing at the same time. My savings would carry us for a while, but I'm twenty-seven, savings aren't a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the extras straight away, no overseas trip next year, and I'd move some of my shares into cash so I'm not caught if the market goes mad. Tomás and I were talking about having a baby in a couple of years, and I think we'd put that on hold until we knew what was what. I'd go to every union meeting and I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground moving under your feet. I've felt that once underground, a small seismic event, and it's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' notice, what would you do in the time before it lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get my safety tickets and certificates all up to date, because if there are any human jobs left on a mine site, they'll be in checking the machines. And I'd talk to my union about getting a deal signed before the robots arrive, not after. Two years is about how long it takes the company to fix a leaking pipe on level nine. That's how fast it'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned putting off having a baby. Is that something you'd really change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. I wouldn't want to bring a kid in while I had no idea if either of us would have work. Tomás might be fine, but I wouldn't risk it on a maybe.

S2.say: She'd say the government must step in quickly with income support for people pushed out. At the safety committee she'd ask who's accountable for checking the robots' work, and she'd share much more online.
S2.think: She thinks her job would be gone within two years along with the nearby mining jobs she'd move to. Her savings would carry them for a while, but at twenty-seven savings aren't a career.
S2.do: Cuts extras straight away, cancels next year's overseas trip and moves some shares into cash. Puts off plans for a baby with Tomás, gets all her safety tickets up to date and pushes the union to sign a deal before the robots arrive.
S2.feel: Like the ground moving under her feet, the way it did once in a small seismic event underground.
S2.quote: Two years is about how long it takes the company to fix a leaking pipe on level nine. That's how fast it'd be.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture is the only one where she changes her family plans; putting off a baby is a big, concrete signal. Her one career hope is in checking and certifying machines. She compares the speed of change to the company's slow pipe repairs, which says a lot about her trust in their planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying we've got five years, so let's use them: training money, a plan for the town, and a rule that the company pays into it. At work I'd want it on the agenda at every safety committee. With friends I'd be less doom and gloom than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me to get one step ahead, if I'm careful. Not enough to do a whole new degree, but enough for a proper qualification in something. My job still goes, but I wouldn't be caught standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the tele-remote course and also start looking at a mine safety inspector qualification, which is about two years part-time. I'd keep saving, aim for eighteen months of expenses by the time it lands. The baby we'd maybe still have, but a bit later, once I'd finished the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Like before an exam you've actually studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years instead of two change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between being pushed and stepping. With five years I can finish a qualification before the door shuts. With two I'd be standing in the doorway holding a half-done certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a safety inspector job even exist if robots do the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. I'd hope the government still wants a human signing off that a mine is safe. If they don't, then I'd have spent two years on something useless, and that's the worry I'd carry.

S3.say: She'd say there are five years, so use them: training money, a plan for the town and company contributions to pay for it. She'd want it at every safety committee and would sound less gloomy than with two years.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to get one step ahead if she's careful: not a degree, but a proper qualification. Her job still goes, but she wouldn't be caught standing still.
S3.do: Does the tele-remote course in the first year and starts a two-year part-time mine safety inspector qualification. Saves towards eighteen months of expenses and pushes the baby back until the course is done.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, like the nerves before an exam she has studied for.
S3.quote: With five years I can finish a qualification before the door shuts. With two I'd be standing in the doorway holding a half-done certificate.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years let her switch from defending her seat to building a next step, the inspector qualification. She's honest that she doesn't know whether that role survives AGI. Family plans are delayed, not cancelled, in this version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this right, and if the company and the government waste it, that's on them. At work I'd be pushing for training to start now, not in year nine. With friends I'd be fairly upbeat, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is a lot. I'd be thirty-seven, I could have finished the inspector qualification, maybe even moved into something different. I'd still worry about the crew, but I'd feel like I had a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep running the loader for now and keep saving. Do the tele-remote course when it's offered, probably year two, then start the safety inspector qualification around year three. We'd go ahead with the baby on our own timeline, because ten years is long enough to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will use the time as an excuse to do nothing. My dad's town had the textile mill closing for a decade and everyone knew, and they still had no plan on the day. Ten years is long enough for everyone to get comfortable and forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you being one of the people who forgets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing it down, honestly. I'd set myself a deadline, like I'll have the inspector ticket by thirty-two. Tomás is good at holding me to things like that.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a real chance to do this right, and wasting it would be on the company and government. At work she'd push for training to start now, and with friends she'd sound fairly upbeat.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is a lot: by thirty-seven she could have finished the inspector qualification or moved somewhere new. She'd worry about the crew but feel she had a path.
S4.do: Keeps running the loader and saving, takes the tele-remote course around year two and starts the inspector qualification around year three. Goes ahead with having a baby on their own timeline.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for everyone to get comfortable and forget.
S4.fieldNote: Her main fear with ten years is complacency, drawn from her dad's town and its slow mill closure. She sets herself a concrete deadline and leans on Tomás to keep her to it. Family plans return to normal once there's enough time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of the money, we'd be okay for a while, but because nothing would be ready, not the training, not the rules, nothing. What would help is the company paying for training before the machines arrive, and a government income support that you don't have to beg for. Down a mine you don't get to wait for proof that the roof is falling. I'd like the same rule for this.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but a mine half full of robots and half full of people is a dangerous place. Someone has to think about that, not just the money.

headlineQuote: Down a mine you don't get to wait for proof that the roof is falling. I'd like the same rule for this.
portrait: Amira is a 27-year-old underground loader operator at a copper mine and her crew's health and safety rep, living with her partner Tomás, a primary teacher. She has about ten months saved plus shares, and uses a chat tool now and then for her safety reports. She welcomes remote machines on dangerous ground but likes others to test new things first. Her biggest change across the scenarios is family: she'd put off having a baby if AGI came in two years, delay it with five, and go ahead with ten. Her path forward is a mine safety inspector qualification.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because neither the training nor the rules would be ready in time.
whatWouldHelp: The company paying for training before the machines arrive, and government income support people don't have to beg for.
